name: Marx's uncritical nineteenth-century belief in inevitable progress
plain_explanation: Like most people of his century, Marx assumed history was moving in a generally upward direction, which let him treat the coming of Socialism as automatically an improvement without needing to argue for it on ethical grounds.
precise_definition: Russell's diagnosis that Marx's confinement of philosophical purview to Man on this one planet, combined with a Copernican failure to register humanity's lack of cosmic importance, produced an unexamined readiness to believe in progress as a universal law, allowing him to dispense with ethics: 'If Socialism was coming, it must be an improvement.'
why_it_mattered: Russell treats this as Marx's gravest philosophical shortcoming: an atheist who nonetheless 'retained a cosmic optimism which only theism could justify.'
historical_origin: A characteristic assumption of nineteenth-century thought generally, shared by Marx's contemporaries.
objections: Russell: 'Broadly speaking, all the elements in Marx's philosophy which are derived from Hegel are unscientific, in the sense that there is no reason whatever to suppose them true.'
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Bears on the relation between Marx's professed atheism and his implicit quasi-religious optimism.
